name: Backgammon Galaxy
tagline: Online backgammon with rated matches, tournaments, bot analysis and a global ladder.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The backgammon part is a solved problem: rules, the doubling cube, Crawford, match equity, even a respectable bot are all well documented and an agent can get you a playable board in a session. What you cannot generate is a few thousand rated humans logging in at 9pm who want a seven point match right now, plus a rating you care about losing. Backgammon Galaxy sells matchmaking liquidity, an ELO-style ladder with history, tournaments and the social pressure that makes a game feel like a sport. A local build gives you practice against a machine, which is useful, and nothing else. If you only ever wanted to drill checker plays and cube decisions against a bot, build it; if you wanted opponents, you are buying the room, not the software.
coreLoopDIY: A local backgammon board that plays full match games against a heuristic bot with full doubling cube and Crawford handling, and logs every move for review.
requirements: Node and a browser, nothing else
Patience for bot tuning: a naive evaluator plays badly in the bear-off and the cube decisions will be the worst part
Optionally a match equity table, which you can hardcode
whatYouLose: Human opponents at any hour, which is the entire product
A rating that means something because other people share it
Tournaments, leagues and events with stakes
Strong neural bot play and the error-rate analysis built on it
Mobile apps, spectating, chat, friend lists
moatNotes: Rating systems only matter when everyone agrees on one. That agreement is the asset, not the code that computes it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Backgammon is a two player game and the scarce resource is the second player, ideally one of roughly your strength, available now, who will see the match through instead of abandoning at 4 away. Platforms that reach that density are rare, and once your rating and match history live somewhere you stop shopping. The paid tier is really a cover charge for the room plus unlimited access to analysis you do not want to maintain yourself.
notes: A playable board is a weekend; a populated lobby is not. The moat is matchmaking liquidity and a shared rating ladder that only works because everyone else is already on it.
prompt:
Build a local, offline backgammon trainer as a single page web app. No accounts, no server, no telemetry, no network calls at all.

Stack, non negotiable: TypeScript, Vite, React, plain CSS. No UI library. No backend. State lives in memory and persists to localStorage.

Game engine, in src/engine, pure functions with no React imports:
- Full backgammon rules: 15 checkers per side, standard starting position, dice rolls, doubles give four moves, hitting and the bar, entering from the bar, blocked points, bear-off only when all checkers are home, exact-or-higher bear-off rule.
- Legal move generation that enforces using the maximum number of dice possible.
- Doubling cube: offer, take, drop, beaver off by default, cube ownership tracking.
- Match play to a configurable length with Crawford rule, gammons and backgammons scored correctly.
- A hardcoded match equity table for cube decisions up to 11 point matches.

Bot, in src/bot:
- One pluggable interface: chooseMove(position, dice) and cubeDecision(position, cube).
- Implement a 1-ply evaluator scoring pip count, blots weighted by hit probability, points made in the home board, anchors, and primes, then a short random rollout for bear-off and race positions.
- Expose a difficulty slider that adds noise to the evaluation.

UI:
- SVG board, click a checker then click a destination, legal destinations highlighted, undo until you commit the turn.
- Cube as a clickable element, clear prompts for take or drop.
- Match score, pip counts, cube state, and a move log in standard notation.
- Hotseat two player mode as a toggle.

Also include: export the current match log as text, import a position via a simple XGID-style string if cheap, otherwise skip it and say so in the README.

Out of scope, do not build: online play, matchmaking, ratings, chat, tournaments, user accounts, neural network training.

Ship a README with how to run it and an honest paragraph on how weak the bot is compared to a real neural evaluator.
